Table 11 summarizes the utility peak hours for eight representative U.S. cities, one per ASHRAE climate zone. Since the utility peak periods extend beyond the TES 2-hour operating window, a subset of the utility peak hours was selected for discharge operation, ensuring the cooling (heating) discharge operating window occurs at the most extreme (highest in cooling, lowest in heating) ambient temperatures, which is expected to result in the largest possible demand reduction. To minimize the recharge energy requirement, the coolest (warmest) nighttime hours were selected in cooling (heating) modes [37], [96]. Of the selected locations, two require additional discussion: (i) Honolulu, HI, representing all-year-round cooling due to its tropical climate, and (ii) Fairbanks, AK, a location without a daily utility peak period, thereby providing the freedom to select the most suitable hours “thermodynamically”, i.e., based on ambient temperatures alone, to discharge and recharge the TES.
